Holzbaurechner / Deck joists

Deck joist calculator

Joists and pedestals for the frame of a deck, whether you lay timber or composite boards on top. The length is measured along the boards.

How the deck frame is built

The 45 × 70 mm joists stand on edge across the direction of the boards. The joist centres depend on the boards: 500 mm is usual for timber boards 25 to 28 mm thick, composite usually needs 400 mm. Underneath sit adjustable pedestals or deck pads that set the height and the fall.

Need the boards as well? Then use the decking calculator, which works out both together.

Single layer or two layers?

With a single layer each joist sits directly on its own pedestals. That is the usual solution on level, well-compacted ground.

With two layers there are also 70 × 70 mm bearers underneath that run in the direction of the boards. The joists sit across them. This needs fewer supports and copes better with uneven ground, but it builds about 70 mm higher. Water can also drain well in both directions.

Protecting the timber by design

The joists must never sit in water or directly on soil. A sub-base of hardcore and gravel with weed membrane, a fall of 1 to 2 % and enough air under the frame make sure everything dries quickly. The frame should last at least as long as the boards on top.

Frequently asked questions

What joist spacing do composite deck boards need?
Composite boards usually require 350 to 400 mm centres, some products even less. The manufacturer's fitting instructions always decide.
How many deck pedestals do I need per m²?
With joists at 500 mm centres and supports every 600 mm, you need just over 3 pedestals per square metre. With two layers it is noticeably fewer.
Which timber is best for deck joists?
Larch and Douglas fir are proven, pressure-treated softwood is cheaper. What matters is that the frame does not rot faster than the boards on top. Under hardwood boards, hardwood or aluminium joists are often used for that reason.
Can I build a deck frame on the lawn?
Not directly. Remove the turf and topsoil, lay a compacted sub-base of hardcore and gravel and put weed membrane on top. Only then do the pedestals go down.

All timber sections are guide values and do not replace a structural calculation. Carports and patio covers may need planning permission and building regulations approval, and a structural engineer's check depending on where you live.
